notes:
Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the material gathered. I have extensive content from Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic), Bible.org (evangelical scholarly), Precept Austin (with John MacArthur's Baptist/Reformed-leaning view, and the major interpretive debate), and Pulpit Commentary (classic Anglican).

---

# Luke 21 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## vv. 1–4: The Widow's Offering

**v. 1:** Jesus "looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the treasury." The Pulpit Commentary notes that the treasury was located in the Court of the Women, with thirteen trumpet-shaped boxes (called *shopheroth*) set in the wall for receiving alms, some marked with inscriptions designating their destination. Jesus sat in the covered colonnade, perhaps resting after His denunciation of the scribes and Pharisees (Luke 20:45–47). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

**v. 2:** "A poor widow put in two small copper coins." The Greek word *lepton* means "a tiny thing"; the Old English "mite" comes from a word for "crumb." The two mites together were about 1% of a denarius (one day's wage), and two mites was the smallest legal offering that could be dropped into the trumpet. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

Luke's word for "poor" (*penichros*, used only here in the NT) differs from Mark's more common word, and suggests she was needy but not a beggar, compelled to work for her scanty maintenance. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/21.htm

**v. 3:** Jesus says she "has put in more than all the others" — not more than any one of them, but more than all of them combined. God measures gifts by what they cost the giver, not by their size. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

**v. 4:** "She out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on." The traditional reading sees this as Jesus' commendation of her sacrificial, wholehearted giving — a beautiful act of devotion. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

**MAJOR INTERPRETIVE DEBATE:** Precept Austin extensively documents a sharply different reading promoted by John MacArthur. MacArthur argues the widow's gift is not a commendation but a *tragic* example: she gave everything to a corrupt, apostate religious system that Jesus had just condemned (Luke 20:47 — scribes "devour widows' houses"). Jesus is not praising her but lamenting that the temple system has taken her last coins. The story sits *between* condemnation of the scribes (20:45–47) and the prophecy of the temple's destruction (21:5–6), forming a bridge of judgment. MacArthur notes the text is silent about her heart motive. The traditional view — held by Calvin, and nearly all older commentators — reads Jesus' words as genuine praise. The IVP Women's Bible Commentary also calls the traditional interpretation "problematic," asking: "Shouldn't the religious establishment be supporting the widow?" — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-21-commentary

Bible.org takes the traditional positive view: Luke casts the widow as setting "the standard of sacrificial giving that all disciples should emulate." — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

## vv. 5–6: The Temple's Destruction Foretold

**v. 5:** The disciples remark on the temple's beauty. Josephus wrote that the temple was covered on the outside with gold plates so brilliant they were blinding in sunlight, and where there was no gold, blocks of pure white marble made travellers think there was snow on the mount. King Herod's rebuilding began in 19 BC and was completed only in AD 63 — just seven years before its destruction. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

**v. 6:** "Not one stone will be left on another; every one will be thrown down." This was fulfilled in AD 70 with remarkable literalness. When Roman soldiers set fire to the temple, gold ornamentation melted and ran into cracks between the stones. To retrieve the gold, the Roman commander ordered the temple dismantled stone by stone. Josephus wrote that except for Herod's three towers and part of the western wall, the city was so thoroughly levelled that no one would believe it had ever been inhabited. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

## vv. 7–11: Signs Before the End

**v. 7:** "When will these things happen? And what will be the sign?" Mark 13:3 identifies the questioners as Peter, James, John, and Andrew. They associated the temple's fall with the glorious manifestation of the Messiah. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

Bible.org notes that Luke focuses on the destruction of Jerusalem, while Matthew and Mark focus on the end of the age. Jesus merges these two topics; Luke seems to emphasize a delayed Second Coming. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 8:** "See to it that you are not deceived." Jesus warns against false messiahs. Josephus records many such impostors in the period before AD 70: Theudas, Simon Magus, Dositheus, Menander, and the "Egyptian" mentioned in Acts 21:38. Bar Kokhba, about 100 years after Jesus, led a widespread revolution and was widely considered the messiah. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

**v. 9:** "Do not be alarmed … the end is not imminent." Wars and rebellions are not the specific sign of the end. Matthew 24:8 calls these "the beginning of birth pains." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

**vv. 10–11:** Nation against nation, earthquakes, famines, pestilences, fearful sights, great signs from heaven. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the period between the Crucifixion and AD 70 was "rich in disasters": earthquakes in Palestine, Italy, Greece, Asia Minor, Crete, and Syria; famines such as the one in Acts 11:28; and portents such as a comet shaped like a sword seen over Jerusalem. Tacitus described the era as "rich in disasters, horrible with battles, torn with seditions, savage even in peace itself." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

## vv. 12–19: Persecution Foretold

**v. 12:** "But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you." The Pulpit Commentary notes two ways to understand "before": either temporally ("prior to these events") or with the sense of "more important than" — i.e., "more important for you as signs will be the trials you endure." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

**v. 13:** "This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses." Persecution opens doors for testimony before people otherwise unreachable — a theme demonstrated throughout Acts. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

**vv. 14–15:** "Do not worry beforehand how to defend yourselves … I will give you speech and wisdom." The Greek *promeletan* ("to prepare beforehand") was a technical term for practising a speech in advance. Instances of this promise include Stephen's speech (Acts 7) and Paul before Felix and Agrippa (Acts 25–26). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

**v. 16:** "Betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you will be put to death." Literally fulfilled for several of the apostles then listening. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

**v. 17:** "Hated by everyone because of My name." Bible.org calls "everyone" a hyperbole (exaggeration). Early Christians were accused of atheism, treason, incest, and cannibalism because of misunderstandings about their doctrines and worship. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 18:** "Yet not even a hair of your head will perish." Not literal (since v. 16 says some will die). Bengel's paraphrase: "Not a hair of your head shall perish without the special providence of God, nor without reward, nor before the due time." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

John Piper at Desiring God uses this verse as a key example of how Jesus' sweeping promises must be understood in light of other Scripture: Jesus promises some will be put to death (v. 16), then immediately says not a hair will perish (v. 18). The promise is about ultimate, eternal security — not freedom from physical harm. — https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/does-god-promise-to-feed-and-clothe-christians

**v. 19:** "By your patient endurance you will gain your souls." The Greek *hupomone* means strong, active endurance, not passive waiting. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

## vv. 20–24: The Destruction of Jerusalem

**v. 20:** "When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near." This is the *specific* sign for the city's fall, distinct from the general signs of vv. 8–11. Vespasian subdued Palestine as Nero's general; after Nero's death and a chaotic year of three emperors, Vespasian became emperor and his son Titus destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70 after a five-month siege that began in April when the city was flooded with Passover pilgrims. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

**v. 21:** "Let those in Judea flee to the mountains." Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* 3.5.2–3) records that Christians in Jerusalem heeded this warning and fled to Pella in the Decapolis across the Jordan. Few if any Christians perished in the fall of Jerusalem. Jews, by contrast, kept trusting in deliverance and stayed — with disastrous results. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/; https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 22:** "These are the days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written." The Pulpit Commentary notes that Deuteronomy 28:15–68 contains almost every form of calamity that visited the Jews during the Roman-Jewish war. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

**v. 23:** "How miserable … for pregnant and nursing mothers!" The woe reflects the difficulty of rapid flight. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 24:** "They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all the nations." Josephus reports 1,100,000 killed and 97,000 taken prisoner and sold as slaves throughout the empire. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

"And Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled." The Pulpit Commentary says "the times of the Gentiles" denotes the whole period between the destruction of Jerusalem and the beginning of the end when the Lord returns — the epoch during which Gentiles hold the place of favour that once belonged to Israel. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic) links this to Daniel 9 and a future seven-year tribulation period: after the "times of the Gentiles" are completed, the final period appointed to Israel begins. He notes that although a Jewish state was re-established in 1948 and Jerusalem regained in 1967, the Temple Mount is still under Gentile control (the Palestinian Authority), so Jerusalem remains "trampled by Gentiles" in a prophetic sense. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

GotQuestions.org (evangelical) explains the "times of the Gentiles" began with Nebuchadnezzar's conquest in 588 BC and continues through the present. Romans 11:25 ("until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in") hints that God's purpose in this era is the worldwide spread of the gospel — aided by things like the Greek language and Roman roads in the first century. — https://www.gotquestions.org/times-of-the-Gentiles.html

## vv. 25–28: The Coming of the Son of Man

**v. 25:** "Signs in the sun and moon and stars … dismay among the nations, bewildered by the roaring of the sea." The Pulpit Commentary notes that Jesus now turns from the near event (AD 70) to the far event (His return). The language echoes Isaiah 13:10 (judgment on Babylon) and Ezekiel 32:7 (judgment on Egypt). Godet likens the earth before the Second Coming to "a ship creaking in every timber at the moment of its going to pieces." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

**v. 26:** "Men will faint from fear … for the powers of the heavens will be shaken." Bible.org says if this is a "visitation of YHWH" context, it refers to creation convulsing at the approach of its Creator. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 27:** "They will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory." The cloud recalls the Shekinah glory of the Pentateuch, the Mount of Transfiguration, and the Ascension (Acts 1:9). Bible.org notes this seems to refer to *all mankind* seeing Him, which precludes a secret rapture. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm

**v. 28:** "When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near." For believers, these terrifying cosmic signs are cause for hope, not fear. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

## vv. 29–33: The Parable of the Fig Tree

**vv. 29–30:** "Look at the fig tree and all the trees." Luke uniquely adds "and all the trees," broadening the parable beyond Israel (the fig tree often symbolises Israel). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

**v. 31:** "When you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near." Just as budding leaves signal summer, these signs signal the fulfilment of God's kingdom. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 32:** "This generation will not pass away until all these things have happened." This is one of the most debated verses in the chapter. Bible.org outlines two major interpretations: (1) "generation" refers to the generation alive in Jesus' day who would witness the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70; (2) "generation" refers to the generation that sees the signs of vv. 25–27 begin — i.e., the final generation. Both interpretations fit the context because Jesus merges the near and far events. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 33:** "Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away." Jesus asserts the absolute, enduring authority of His words — greater than even the created order. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

## vv. 34–36: Exhortation to Watchfulness

**v. 34:** "Watch yourselves, or your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life." Bible.org notes this is addressed to the Apostles themselves — the Christian life is a "tension-filled pilgrimage," and many believers have damaged their witness through the temptations and cares of this age. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 35:** "For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of all the earth." The judgment is universal in scope. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 36:** "Keep watch at all times, and pray that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man." Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic) connects this to the rapture: believers who are ready will be "counted worthy to escape" the coming tribulation, while the unprepared will be caught by His coming like a snare (v. 34–35). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

Bible.org notes a Greek manuscript variant: some manuscripts read "counted worthy to escape" (*kataxiōthēte*, MSS A, C, D), while others read "have strength to escape" (*katischusēte*, MSS א, B, L, W). The UBS4 committee prefers the latter reading ("have strength"). — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

## vv. 37–38: Summary of Jesus' Final Days

**v. 37:** "Every day Jesus taught at the temple, but every evening He went out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives." Jesus camped on the Mount of Olives during His final week — a place well known to Judas and the site of Jesus' arrest. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**v. 38:** "Early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple." Jesus' popularity with both Passover pilgrims and locals was one reason the religious leaders feared Him and sought to arrest Him away from the crowds. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

---

# Denominational Differences & Other Views

## The Widow's Mite (vv. 1–4): Traditional vs. MacArthur's Reading

**Traditional (Calvin, Pulpit Commentary, most pastors):** The widow is a model of sacrificial, wholehearted devotion. Her giving "won the Lord's praise" and "has touched the hearts of so many generations." God measures gifts by what they cost the giver. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-21-commentary (citing Calvin)

**John MacArthur (Baptist/Reformed-leaning, via Precept Austin):** The widow is a tragic figure, giving her last coins to a corrupt religious system Jesus had just condemned. The story is *not* about principles of giving but continues the theme of judgment from Luke 20:47 ("scribes devour widows' houses") into the temple's destruction (21:5–6). The text is silent about her heart or motive. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-21-commentary

**Hybrid view (Geoffrey Smith, Presbyterian, JETS):** The passage functions on two levels — it genuinely commends the widow's devotion *and* it forms a thematic bridge between condemnation of the scribes and the temple's coming destruction. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-21-commentary

## "This Generation" (v. 32)

**Preterist/partial-preterist:** "This generation" means the generation alive in Jesus' day, and "all these things" refers to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (except the Second Coming elements, which are still future). — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

**Futurist/Dispensational (e.g., Enduring Word):** "This generation" means the generation that sees the signs of vv. 25–27 begin — the final generation before Christ's return. — implicit in https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

## "Escape All These Things" (v. 36) — Rapture or Endurance?

**Pre-tribulation rapture view (Pentecostal/charismatic, Enduring Word):** Verse 36 promises believers will be "counted worthy to escape" the coming tribulation via the rapture. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-21/

**Alternative evangelical view (Bible.org):** The Greek textual evidence favours "have strength to escape" rather than "counted worthy." The emphasis is on prayerful readiness, not a specific mechanism of escape. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-21

## Not a Hair Will Perish (v. 18) — Ultimate Security

**John Piper (Reformed Baptist, Desiring God):** This verse, placed right after "some of you will be put to death," demonstrates that God's promises of protection are about *ultimate*, eternal security — not exemption from physical suffering. This principle also governs promises about food, clothing, and other needs. — https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/does-god-promise-to-feed-and-clothe-christians

**Traditional (Pulpit Commentary, citing Bengel):** "Not a hair of your head shall perish without the special providence of God, nor without reward, nor before the due time." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/21.htm
